scenario: Community search over short user-generated posts, questions, answers and comments. Key metrics are search relevance (nDCG) and CTR. Focus: semantic matching, query understanding, short-text retrieval, ranking models, and LLM applications in search.

papers.title: ForkPilot: Self-Evolving Policy for Retrospective Search in Long-Horizon Agents
papers.authors: Xinyue Zeng, Shivam Shandilya, Guilherme Potje, Leonardo Nunes, Rakshanda Agarwal, Ranveer Chandra, Emre Kiciman, Dawei Zhou, Tusher Chakraborty
papers.summary: In long-horizon agent tasks, one failed tool call early on makes the later steps fail with it. Retrospective search repairs this by going back to a recoverable earlier state in the failed trajectory, keeping the correct actions before it, and forking a new run from there. The hard part is deciding when to fork and how many times: the reward only arrives when the task ends, and every fork costs extra tokens. ForkPilot builds labels from trajectories that have already finished: from the same state, it runs one continuation with a fork and one without to the end, and uses the difference in final score minus the difference in token cost as the label for whether that fork was worth it; it then trains a predictor that scores candidate fork options. At deployment it forks only when the lower bound of the predicted gain is above zero, and after each finished task it adds the new trajectories to the training set and refits. ==What it learns is whether this step is worth extra compute; the agent's own action policy stays untouched==. On 6 benchmarks and 4 open-source models, compared with full Retrospective Tree Search (RTS), it uses 36.2% fewer raw tokens on average while scoring 0.23 points higher on average.
papers.abstract: Interactive language-model agents increasingly solve complex tasks through long-horizon, multi-call reasoning, where errors in beliefs or actions can compound across tool interactions. Retrospective search can recover from such failures but is prone to misallocation. Delayed outcomes obscure the contribution of intermediate search decisions, leading to Attribution Complexity, while evolving execution evidence leads to Adaptation Complexity, where previously learned estimates become stale. To address these challenges, we first introduce Search Value Dynamics (SVD), which characterizes the evolving trade-off between the gain and cost of retrospective search. Building on SVD, we propose ForkPilot, a self-evolving two-stage policy-learning framework. In the first stage, ForkPilot learns a search-value policy offline from completed trajectories through automatically constructed outcome comparisons. In the second stage, it makes search decisions based on current observations and then self-evolves by incorporating newly completed trajectories into subsequent policy updates. We evaluate ForkPilot across 6 diverse benchmarks and 7 widely used LLM backbone families, including four open-source families, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Opus 4.8 in a production agentic system, against 9 competitive baselines, including a real-world harness deployment used by hundreds of thousands of paid users. ForkPilot achieves comparable state-of-the-art performance while reducing token usage by up to 59.2%, demonstrating its efficacy.

deep_reading.title: ForkPilot: Self-Evolving Policy for Retrospective Search in Long-Horizon Agents
deep_reading.content:
Long-horizon agent tasks call tools dozens of times in a row, and when one early judgment is wrong, the later steps keep working on top of the wrong premise. Retrospective search repairs this as follows: after a task fails, the agent reviews the whole trajectory, finds a recoverable earlier state, keeps the correct actions before it, and forks a new execution from there. The problem is that this search is expensive, and it is hard to decide in advance when to fork, how many times to fork and which trajectory to keep searching. With GPT-5.6 Sol on AutomationBench, a single agent run scores 43.7, and full Retrospective Tree Search (RTS) reaches 77.0, but its inference cost per task is also clearly higher. ForkPilot, from Microsoft and Virginia Tech, learns an allocation policy: at each moment where a fork is possible, it predicts whether "the extra score from this fork minus the extra token cost" is above zero, and it forks only if it is. On 6 benchmarks and 4 open-source models, compared with RTS it uses 36.2% fewer raw tokens on average while scoring 0.23 points higher on average. ==It only changes how much compute goes into retrospection; how the agent itself acts at each step is left unchanged==, so it can wrap around an existing agent.

Below, I first explain why retrospective search is hard to allocate, then what each of ForkPilot's two stages does, and then three main experiments and two check experiments.

## 1. The problem: whether a fork was worth it is only known when the task ends

![Left: an example of retrospective search. While rotating hospital-system keys, the agent wrongly believes all stores have migrated to the new key; after it disables the old key, reading the archive fails. During retrospection it queries the key bindings, finds that the archive still uses the old key, and forks from an earlier state to migrate the archive before disabling the old key. Right: task score versus inference cost per task for GPT-5.6 Sol on AutomationBench. ForkPilot (red star) scores 75.0, close to RTS's 77.0, at lower cost, and sits on the Pareto frontier (paper Figure 1).](figs/2610.04889/fig1_retrospective_pareto.png)

Retrospective search in long-horizon tasks has two concrete difficulties, and the authors gave each a name.

The first is Attribution Complexity. The effect of a fork only becomes visible after all later tool calls have run and the final reward arrives, and the final reward is shaped both by this fork and by every action after it. Making the same kind of fork from the same state produces final-score differences that vary widely, because sampling randomness and environment feedback differ. Estimating the average value of a fork accurately therefore needs many pairs of finished samples.

The second is Adaptation Complexity. New observations and search results change the current state, and the live environment itself changes too. What was learned on the previous batch of tasks, "forking pays off in this situation", may no longer hold on a new task.

The authors write the quantity to be estimated as a paired comparison. At decision point $t$, a candidate allocation $u$ specifies the number of forks and the maximum depth of each branch, and $u^0$ means no fork, continuing the current execution. Starting from the same restored state, the system runs to the end of the task once under $u$ and once under $u^0$:

$$G_t(u)=\mathbb{E}\big[\,R(x,\tau_t^u)-R(x,\tau_t^0)-\lambda\,(C(\tau_t^u)-C(\tau_t^0))\;\big|\;z_t\big]$$

Here $R$ is the task reward (0 to 1), $C$ is the token cost, including the generation and evaluation cost of branches that were not selected, $\lambda$ converts cost into reward units, and $z_t$ is the summary of what the controller can see at that moment: the actions and observations so far, the branches already explored and their outcomes, and the remaining budget. Intuitively, $G_t(u)>0$ means the extra score from this fork exceeds the extra cost. The authors call this characterization Search Value Dynamics (SVD). The paper also gives a bound showing that when an estimate fitted on old tasks is applied to a new state, the error comes from three parts: sampling error from too few samples, the change in the input state, and the change in the reward distribution itself. The authors state explicitly that this bound only explains why the two difficulties exist and provides no guarantee for the deployed controller.

## 2. Method: learn scores offline, decide by the lower bound online

ForkPilot has two stages. The first stage updates parameters between tasks; the second stage makes decisions inside a single task with the parameters fixed.

**Stage I: build labels from finished trajectories.** At a source-task state where a fork is possible, the system runs both "fork under $u$" and "no fork" to the end, obtaining a score difference $\tilde Y$ and a normalized cost difference $\tilde D$. Each pair labels only the allocation that was selected, and no human labels of the form "fork this many times here" are needed. The model is an encoder that turns $z_t$ into a vector, followed by $M$ prediction heads trained on task bootstrap samples; each head takes the vector and a candidate allocation and outputs a predicted score difference and cost difference. Averaging the heads gives the net-value estimate $\hat G_t(u)$.

A point estimate alone is not enough, because the two difficulties in Section 1 make the estimate inaccurate. ForkPilot trains an additional error model that predicts an upper quantile $\hat\beta_t(u)$ of the net-value estimation error; its inputs include the disagreement among the prediction heads, how close the current state is to the training data, and residuals on held-out samples, and it is calibrated on a separate set of source data. This gives a lower bound $L_t(u)=\hat G_t(u)-\hat\beta_t(u)$ and an upper bound $U_t(u)=\hat G_t(u)+\hat\beta_t(u)$. The authors stress that these two values are only decision scores, not coverage guarantees.

**Stage II: closed-loop decisions inside a task.** At every moment where a fork is possible, the controller scores all candidate allocations using the current $z_t$, with three tiers of rules:

1. If some allocation has a lower bound above zero, fork with the one whose lower bound is largest.
2. If no lower bound is above zero but some "small probe" allocation has an upper bound above zero, pick, among these probes, the one with the smallest predicted cost difference. The probes' fork count and depth caps are set in advance and are stricter than the limits the system allows.
3. Otherwise, skip this round and continue the current execution.

==The second tier spends a little to try when the outcome is uncertain but may pay off==, and the new observations from the probe update $z_t$, so the next decision has more information. After a task ends, its decisions, branches, outcomes and costs are added to the experience pool, and Stage I refits the parameters on the enlarged pool; this is the "self-evolving" in the title.

An illustrative example (numbers are illustrative): at some moment, the candidate allocation "fork 2 branches, at most 5 steps each" has a predicted net value of 0.06 and an error upper quantile of 0.10, so its lower bound is negative and its upper bound positive; the probe allocation "fork 1 branch, at most 2 steps" has a positive upper bound and the lowest predicted cost. The controller picks this probe; it neither gives up outright nor launches a large search directly.

## 3. Core contributions

- It formulates retrospective search in long-horizon tasks as an allocation problem defined by "score difference minus cost difference", and splits the difficulty into two kinds, attribution and adaptation.
- It trains the allocation policy with labels built automatically from paired replay, with no human labels of the optimal allocation and no need for paired replay at every step during deployment.
- It handles estimation uncertainty with three tiers of rules, lower bound, probe and skip, and updates parameters with new trajectories after every task.

## 4. Experiments

The experiments compare 9 baselines in three groups: test-time search (BoN-5, which samples 5 times and keeps the best; full Retrospective Tree Search RTS; Retrospective Depth Search RDS, which continues only from the last resumable node of the first trajectory), experience-based methods (ACE, ReasoningBank, Reflexion, GEPA and Trace2Skill, which use past trajectories to produce reflections, memories or skills), and GitHub Copilot's agent harness GHCP. The 6 benchmarks cover workflow automation (AutomationBench), tool-user interaction (τ³-Bench), software engineering (SWE-bench Verified), multimodal tool use (MM-ToolSandbox), web interaction (WorkArena++) and general interactive tasks (VitaBench). The metrics are task score S (0–100), plus the ratio of raw tokens R and the ratio of uncached tokens U relative to RTS; lower R and U mean more savings.

**Experiment 1: does it save tokens consistently across benchmarks?** The method is to compare ForkPilot with all baselines on the 6 benchmarks on 4 open-source models (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Kimi-K3, DeepSeek-R1-671B, Qwen3.8-27B). The result is that, relative to RTS, raw tokens fall by 36.2% on average, uncached tokens by 30.3% on average, and task score rises by 0.23 points on average; raw-token savings per benchmark range from 31.8% on SWE-bench to 39.8% on AutomationBench. The table below excerpts three benchmarks for Qwen3.8-27B:

| Method | AutomationBench S / R | τ³-Bench S / R | SWE-bench S / R |
|---|---|---|---|
| BoN-5 | 18.0 / 1.07 | 66.4 / 1.13 | 49.2 / 1.10 |
| RTS | 30.5 / 1.00 | 73.8 / 1.00 | 57.6 / 1.00 |
| ACE | 27.8 / 0.56 | 74.2 / 0.50 | 53.8 / 0.59 |
| GEPA | 29.0 / 0.59 | 75.1 / 0.52 | 56.0 / 0.64 |
| Trace2Skill | 28.2 / 0.54 | 73.4 / 0.55 | 55.2 / 0.61 |
| ForkPilot | 31.0 / 0.58 | 74.4 / 0.61 | 58.0 / 0.65 |

The table shows a pattern: experience-based methods such as ACE and GEPA sometimes have lower token ratios than ForkPilot, but their scores are generally below RTS; ForkPilot's scores match RTS or are slightly higher. ==What it saves is the part of RTS's search that does not pay off, so the score does not drop with it==.

**Experiment 2: does the gain hold as model size changes?** The method is to repeat the experiment at four Qwen3.5 sizes, 4B, 9B, 27B and 122B-A10B. The result is that raw-token savings rise from 28.5% at 4B to 33.7% at 9B and 37.0% at 27B, and are 35.8% at 122B-A10B; the score changes relative to RTS at the four sizes are +0.27, +0.27, +0.30 and +0.23 points. The authors read this as the gain saturating at the largest size.

**Experiment 3: does it still save with closed frontier models inside a production system?** The method is to use GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8 inside a production agentic system, on inference platforms with caching, and test two benchmarks, AutomationBench and τ³-Bench.

| Method | Sol Automation S / R / U | Sol τ³ S / R / U | Opus Automation S / R / U | Opus τ³ S / R / U |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BoN-5 | 59.83 / 2.030 / 1.689 | 59.28 / 0.989 / 1.138 | 55.17 / 1.491 / 1.025 | 44.44 / 1.137 / 2.743 |
| RDS | 68.83 / 1.632 / 0.697 | 55.67 / 2.783 / 0.775 | 62.50 / 3.188 / 1.192 | 29.90 / 1.685 / 0.454 |
| GHCP | 33.50 / 0.846 / 0.481 | 43.30 / 0.208 / 0.186 | 39.83 / 0.487 / 0.189 | 41.24 / 0.171 / 0.251 |
| RTS | 71.83 / 1.000 / 1.000 | 67.53 / 1.000 / 1.000 | 70.83 / 1.000 / 1.000 | 44.67 / 1.000 / 1.000 |
| ForkPilot | 69.00 / 0.764 / 0.556 | 64.43 / 0.588 / 0.408 | 66.67 / 0.778 / 0.763 | 48.31 / 0.611 / 0.569 |

The result is that ForkPilot used 58.8–77.8% of RTS's raw tokens and 40.8–76.3% of its uncached tokens; the "up to 59.2% savings" in the abstract refers to the uncached-token saving here. The scores deserve a close look: on both Sol benchmarks and on Opus AutomationBench, ForkPilot is below RTS (69.00 vs 71.83, 64.43 vs 67.53, 66.67 vs 70.83), and only on Opus τ³-Bench is it higher (48.31 vs 44.67). So on closed models it trades part of the score for cost. Compared with RDS, ForkPilot scores higher in all four settings with 53.1–78.9% lower raw cost, ==which shows that the gain comes from choosing the right place to fork; simply searching deeper along one trajectory cannot achieve it==.

**Check 1: does the gain come from leaked evaluator feedback?** The prompt given to the agent during retrospection contains evaluator feedback, and the authors were concerned that the model might use it to "peek at the answer". The method is to remove the feedback and keep only the execution history (masked), or to shuffle the feedback across tasks (shuffled). The result is that on AutomationBench, Qwen3.5-9B scores 14.5 original, 14.4 masked and 13.0 shuffled; Qwen3.5-27B scores 25.6, 25.5 and 23.2. Removing the feedback barely changes the score, which shows that the gain does not come from answer cues in the feedback.

**Check 2: how much experience is needed to learn well?** The method is to learn the policy on AutomationBench with only part of the training data and compute what fraction of the full-training improvement is recovered.

![Task score on AutomationBench as the training-data fraction grows, for three models: the x-axis is the fraction of the training set used for policy learning, and the dashed line marks 25%, where all three models have already recovered 82%–83% of the full improvement; after that the curves flatten (paper Figure 2).](figs/2610.04889/fig2_sample_efficiency.png)

The result is that with only 25% of the training split (13.3% of all data), it recovers 81–85% of the full improvement, and the remaining 75% of the data contributes only another 15–19%.

## 5. Limitations

The authors state that the theoretical bound only explains the two difficulties, attribution and adaptation, and provides no guarantee for the learned error estimate or the deployed controller; the upper and lower error bounds are only decision scores. Two facts to add: first, the method requires the host system to be able to restore earlier environment states, so forking is unavailable for real operations that cannot be rolled back (for example, a request that has already been sent); second, on closed models 3 of the 4 settings score below RTS, so the token savings come at the price of a small amount of score.

## 6. Practical takeaways

- If your agent already uses retries or tree search, ForkPilot's approach can be borrowed directly: record "score difference minus cost difference" for each extra search as a training label and learn a scorer that decides whether to keep searching, with no retraining of the agent itself.
- The three-tier decision rule (search big only when the lower bound is positive, probe small first when the upper bound is positive, skip otherwise) can be used on its own, and suits settings with a fixed compute budget where you do not want to miss searches that might pay off.

Two facts to add: first, the method requires the host system to be able to restore earlier environment states, so forking is unavailable for real operations that cannot be rolled back (for example, a request that has already been sent); second, on closed models 3 of the 4 settings score below RTS, so the token savings come at the price of a small amount of score.

6. Practical takeaways

  • If your agent already uses retries or tree search, ForkPilot's approach can be borrowed directly: record "score difference minus cost difference" for each extra search as a training label and learn a scorer that decides whether to keep searching, with no retraining of the agent itself.
  • The three-tier decision rule (search big only when the lower bound is positive, probe small first when the upper bound is positive, skip otherwise) can be used on its own, and suits settings with a fixed compute budget where you do not want to miss searches that might pay off.

papers.title: Web Search on TokenHub, Tencent Cloud's Model Serving Platform
papers.summary: This is the web-search API documentation for TokenHub, Tencent Cloud's model serving platform. With web search turned on, the model decides by itself whether to search and which keywords to search for while answering, and then generates the answer from the search results. There are two ways to integrate: the Responses API declares a web_search tool in the tools field and returns cited sources in structured annotations; the Chat Completions API turns search on with web_search_options and returns cited sources in search_results. It currently supports Hy3 and the DeepSeek V4 model family, search is priced in two tiers, lite and standard, the limit is 5 QPS, and it is only available in the Guangzhou region. ==For search teams, the reference value is the interface shape: search is packaged as a tool the model calls by itself, and cited sources come back together with the answer==, so an in-house RAG service can align with these fields and make a later switch easier.
papers.abstract: 联网搜索是 TokenHub 提供的模型增强能力。开启后，大模型在回答时可自动调用搜索引擎获取实时网络信息，解决模型知识时效性不足的问题。平台支持 Responses API 与 Chat Completions API 两种协议，模型可自主判断是否需要搜索、搜索什么关键词，并基于搜索结果生成回答，同时通过结构化 annotations 返回引用来源。

papers.title: TeleTune: Evolving Agent Skills From Offline Telemetry
papers.authors: Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Elias Stengel-Eskin, Yan Chen, Pol Llado, Scott Counts, Mohit Bansal, Benjamin Van Durme, Harsh Jhamtani, Gaurav Verma
papers.summary: Computer-use agents need to know how people actually use software. User activity logs (telemetry) are plentiful, but they have three problems: the logs do not record the goal behind each action, past activity cannot be replayed to check whether a skill is good, and several tasks are interleaved in the same log. TeleTune uses the logs themselves as the exam: it has the agent predict the next action on recorded trajectories, proposes edits to a textual skill library based on where the predictions were wrong, and keeps only the edits that raise action-prediction accuracy on held-out trajectories. ==Action-prediction accuracy can be computed offline, so it replaces task success rate, which cannot be measured without replay, as the optimization signal==. At test time the agent receives the learned skill library plus demonstration trajectories retrieved by workflow. On WorkArena and Online-Mind2Web its average success rates are 77.1% and 80.6%, 6.7% and 7.7% above the strongest baseline on each benchmark.
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents need to capture procedural knowledge of how people use software. User telemetry offers a scalable source of this knowledge. However, learning reusable skills from these logs requires addressing three challenges: (1) Goal Underspecification, since logs do not record the goal behind each action; (2) Non-Replayability, since past activity cannot be replayed to evaluate skill updates; and (3) Interleaved Trajectories, since logs may mix several tasks without marking their boundaries. To address these, we introduce TeleTune, a framework for learning a textual skill library from offline logs without recorded goals, cannot be replayed during optimization, and may interleave tasks. TeleTune uses action-prediction errors on logged trajectories to propose library edits and keep only those that improve held-out action-prediction accuracy, which we call skill-guided progress. The learned workflows also enable retrieval of demonstrations that cover the subgoals of a new task. At test time, the agent is provided with the learned library and the workflow-based retrieved demonstrations. Experiments on WorkArena and Online-Mind2Web show that TeleTune outperforms random retrieval, Agent Workflow Memory (AWM), and their combination. We find that the best baseline varies by setting, whereas TeleTune achieves average success rates of 77.1% and 80.6%, respectively, improving over the strongest baseline on each benchmark by 6.7% and 7.7%. Under the heaviest perturbation of the WorkArena training data, TeleTune keeps the highest average success rate at 68.5%, 6.3% above the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Subagents vs Agent Skills: Executing Reusable Knowledge for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
papers.authors: Wasu Top Piriyakulkij, Rachel Lawrence, Alicia Curth, Sushrut Karmalkar, Niranjani Prasad
papers.summary: An agent skill package is a multi-file bundle of instructions, scripts and resources, and the usual way to use one is to load the skill instructions into the main agent's context and let the agent follow them. As tasks get longer, the context keeps piling up and reasoning quality drops. This paper compares another execution mode: invoking the skill package as a subagent, so that each subtask is solved in a fresh context window of its own. On SkillsBench, with the original human-curated skill packages, loading them directly into the context matches or beats subagents; with the authors' synthesized packages that spell out input-output contracts, subagents pull ahead, and the smaller the model, the larger the gain. ==Subagents pay off only when a skill has a clear input-output interface, because the main agent must be able to hand off a subtask completely and then take the result back==. The cost is a clear increase in total tokens, because each subagent has to be given the context it needs all over again.
papers.abstract: How can language model agents effectively leverage libraries of reusable knowledge to solve long-horizon tasks? Recent work has increasingly focused on agent skills: reusable capabilities represented as skill packages, i.e., multi-file bundles containing instructions, scripts, and other resources that help agents perform specific tasks. Agent skills are typically executed by loading their skill instructions into an agent's context and relying on the agent to follow them. As task horizons grow, however, this approach becomes increasingly brittle, because reasoning quality degrades as more information accumulates in the context window. We investigate an alternative approach in which skill packages are instead invoked as subagents. Rather than loading skill instructions into the main context, subagent execution spawns fresh context windows dedicated to solving individual subtasks. We show that subagent execution outperforms agent-skill execution when skill packages expose clear input-output contracts and their instructions encode the procedural knowledge needed to fulfill those contracts. The tradeoff is additional communication overhead, as extra tokens are required to coordinate between the main agent and its subagents.

papers.title: What Is Agentic RAG: How Agents Enhance Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.summary: This is an explainer article on the Alibaba Cloud developer community about what Agentic RAG is. Traditional RAG follows one fixed "retrieve first, then generate" pipeline; Agentic RAG brings an agent into it, which first works out what material the question needs, then decides how to search, whether to search again, and whether to call other tools, and finally composes the answer. The article groups the core mechanisms into five kinds: agent collaboration, external tool calls, reasoning enhancement, query refinement and iterative interaction, and names complex knowledge-base QA, document summarization and multi-step analysis as the use cases. ==The article contains no experiments or numbers, so it is better suited to explaining the concept to business stakeholders==; to judge how well a specific approach works, you need the paper or evaluation of the corresponding system.
papers.abstract: Agentic RAG 可理解为智能体检索增强生成，是在传统 RAG 基础上引入 AI Agent 能力的一类方法。它让智能体参与检索、推理和生成过程，使系统不再只按固定链路完成一次检索和回答，而是能围绕复杂问题主动规划、选择工具、细化查询，并在必要时逐步修正结果。实际系统通常与知识库、检索引擎、模型推理、工具调用和工作流共同组成完整方案。

papers.title: Code Understanding is a Bottleneck for Coding Agents
papers.authors: Nishant Balepur, Kiran Tomlinson, Tobias Schnabel
papers.summary: Repository-level benchmarks for coding agents, such as SWE-bench, often assume that the more lines of code are edited, the harder the task; but these datasets control code and task types poorly, so they cannot show which ability actually causes an agent's errors. CABRA builds tasks from scratch: each task is one transformation of a function call graph, and a single task-size parameter scales difficulty along four directions: traversing functions along the call chain, search, runtime resolution and instruction following. The authors ran 8 LLMs and 6 coding agents on 6,840 CABRA tasks. As tasks grow, plain LLM accuracy falls, while agents offload the work to tools such as grep and stay near-perfect, but their tool calls for reading and analyzing code increase. On SWE-bench Verified trajectories, these tool-call counts predict whether an agent succeeds better than the number of lines edited in the final solution. ==For agents, the difficulty lies more in understanding the code to be changed; making the edit itself is not the bottleneck==.
papers.abstract: Repository benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench) for coding agents often assume that lines of code edited can predict task difficulty, but such datasets' poor control over code and task types makes it hard to know which abilities truly drive agent errors. We present CABRA: a Coding Ability Blueprint for Rigorous Agent evaluation. CABRA builds tasks from scratch as call graph transformations and scales difficulty via a task size parameter on four axes: function traversal, search, runtime resolution, and instruction following. We run eight LLMs and six coding agents on 6,840 CABRA tasks to show: 1) LLM accuracy falls as task size grows, but agents stay near-perfect by offloading work to tools; 2) Larger CABRA tasks elicit more tool calls for reading and analysis, while a separate study on SWE-bench Verified shows these tool call counts predict agents' accuracy better than lines of code edited; 3) Extending CABRA to an intense understanding task where models analyze divergent logic across two classes backs this finding, as agent accuracy finally falls.
